_comment: Short usage notes for tricky words, keyed by the word list's dictionary form (pt). Shown when a learner taps the word.
lhe: 'Lhe' means 'to you / to him / to her' (an indirect object: the person something is given, said or sent to). Eu lhe dou o livro = I give you the book. In everyday Brazilian speech it's fairly formal; people usually say 'pra você' / 'pra ele' instead (Eu dou o livro pra você). You'll still see it in writing, polite speech and set phrases (Eu lhe agradeço).
se: 'Se' has two jobs. As a pronoun it makes a verb reflexive or reciprocal (Ela se chama Ana = she calls herself Ana; Eles se conhecem = they know each other) and appears in impersonal phrases (Aluga-se = for rent; Fala-se português = Portuguese is spoken). As a conjunction it means 'if' (Se chover, eu fico em casa).
me: 'Me' is 'me / to me / myself'. In Brazil it usually goes before the verb: Ele me ajudou (he helped me), Me chamo Ana (I'm called Ana). Starting a sentence with it (Me dá um café) is normal in speech; formal writing prefers Dê-me.
te: 'Te' is 'you / to you / yourself' for 'tu'. Brazilians mix it freely with 'você': Eu te amo, Te vejo amanhã, even when they otherwise say 'você'. It's informal and very common.
nos: 'Nos' is 'us / to us / ourselves' (Ele nos convidou = he invited us). Careful: 'nos' is also em + os (= in the, plural): nos fins de semana = on the weekends. Context tells you which.
o: 'O / a / os / as' are 'the', matching the noun's gender and number: o livro, a casa, os livros, as casas. They also combine with prepositions: do, da (de + o/a), no, na (em + o/a), ao, à (a + o/a), pelo, pela (por + o/a). As pronouns they mean 'him / her / it / them' (Eu o vi = I saw him), but in Brazilian speech people usually say 'Eu vi ele'.
a: 'A' as a preposition means 'to / at' (Vou a Lisboa; às três = at three). It merges with the article: a + o = ao, a + a = à (the grave accent marks this 'crase'). In speech Brazilians often use 'para' or 'em' instead (Vou pra praia, Fui no mercado).
a gente: 'A gente' literally means 'the people' but is used all the time for 'we'. It takes the verb form for ele/ela: A gente vai à praia (= Nós vamos à praia). It's informal but completely normal in Brazil.
você: 'Você' is the everyday 'you' in Brazil, and it takes the ele/ela form of the verb: Você fala português? Plural: vocês (+ eles/elas form). 'Tu' is used in some regions, often still with the você verb form; to be extra polite, use 'o senhor / a senhora'.
de: 'De' means 'of / from' and merges with articles and pronouns: do, da, dos, das (de + o, a…), dele, dela (= his, her: o livro dela = her book), deste, desse, daquele, daqui. Many verbs and phrases need it: gostar de, precisar de, perto de, antes de.
em: 'Em' means 'in / on / at' and merges with articles and pronouns: no, na, nos, nas (em + o, a…), num, numa, nele, nela, neste, nesse, naquele. Moro no Rio, Está na mesa, Penso nele (I think about him).
por: 'Por' means 'through / by / for (in exchange, because of) / per'. With articles: pelo, pela. Passei pelo parque (through the park), Obrigado pela ajuda (thanks for the help), duas vezes por semana. Compare 'para', which points to a destination, purpose or recipient.
para: 'Para' means 'for / to / in order to' and points to a destination, purpose, recipient or deadline: Vou para casa, Isto é para você, Estudo para aprender. In speech it shortens to 'pra' (pra mim, pro Rio = para o Rio).
ser: 'Ser' is 'to be' for what something is: identity, origin, profession, lasting traits, time and dates. Eu sou de Boston, Ela é médica, São três horas. Compare 'estar' for temporary states and locations.
estar: 'Estar' is 'to be' for how or where something is right now: states, feelings, locations, and 'be + -ing' (estou falando). Estou cansada, O café está quente, Onde você está? Compare 'ser' for identity and lasting traits.
ficar: 'Ficar' is versatile: 'to stay' (Fiquei em casa), 'to be located' (O banco fica na esquina), and 'to become / get' with adjectives (Ele ficou feliz = he got happy). Ficar com = to keep / end up with.
ter: 'Ter' means 'to have', and in Brazil also 'there is / there are' in speech: Tem um mercado aqui perto (= Há um mercado…). Ter que / ter de + infinitive = to have to (Tenho que trabalhar).
haver: 'Haver' mostly appears as 'há' = 'there is / there are' (more formal than 'tem') and 'ago' (há dois anos = two years ago). In speech Brazilians usually say 'tem' for 'there is'.
ir: 'Ir' means 'to go'. Its present (vou, vai, vamos, vão) + an infinitive is the everyday future: Vou comer = I'm going to eat. Its past (fui, foi…) is the same as ser's: context tells 'I went' from 'I was'.
já: 'Já' means 'already' (Já comi = I've already eaten), 'ever' in questions (Você já foi ao Rio? = have you ever been to Rio?), and 'right away' (Já vou! = coming!). 'Já não' = not anymore.
ainda: 'Ainda' means 'still' (Ainda moro aqui) and 'yet' with não (Ainda não terminei = I haven't finished yet).
muito: 'Muito' as an adverb (very / a lot) never changes: muito bom, gosto muito. As an adjective (much / many) it agrees with the noun: muita água, muitos livros, muitas pessoas.
bom: 'Bom' is the adjective 'good' (um bom livro, uma boa ideia). 'Bem' is the adverb 'well' (Estou bem, Ela fala bem). Compare: mau / mal (bad / badly).
todo: 'Todo / toda' + article means 'the whole' (todo o dia = the whole day); 'todos / todas' means 'all, every' (todos os dias = every day). 'Tudo' means 'everything' and never changes (Tudo bem?).
que: 'Que' is 'that / which / who' linking clauses (O livro que eu li), 'what' in questions (O que você quer?), and 'than' in comparisons (mais alto que). 'Que bom!' = how nice!
porque: Four spellings: 'por que' = why (in questions: Por que você saiu?), 'porque' = because (Saí porque estava cansado), 'por quê' = why at the end of a question (Você saiu por quê?), 'o porquê' = the reason.
este: Demonstratives: 'este' = this (near me), 'esse' = that (near you), 'aquele' = that over there. In Brazilian speech 'esse' is often used for 'this' too. They merge with de/em: deste, desse, naquele.
esse: 'Esse / essa' = 'that' (near the listener), and in Brazilian speech often 'this' as well. 'Isso' = 'that / this thing' (Isso é bom). Merges: desse, nesse, disso, nisso.
meu: Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: meu livro, minha casa, meus amigos. 'Seu / sua' can mean your, his, her or their, so Brazilians often use 'dele / dela' for his / her (a casa dela).
seu: 'Seu / sua' officially means your, his, her, their, but in Brazil it usually means 'your' (você's). For his / her / their, people say 'dele / dela / deles' after the noun: o carro dele = his car.
onde: 'Onde' = where (Onde você mora?). 'Aonde' = to where, with verbs of motion (Aonde você vai?). In speech many people use 'onde' for both.
aqui: 'Aqui' = here (near me), 'aí' = there (near you), 'ali' = there (nearby), 'lá' = over there (far). Daqui = from here; por aqui = around here.
gostar: 'Gostar' (to like) always takes 'de': Eu gosto de café, Ela gosta do Rio (de + o). Before an infinitive too: Gosto de ler.
acabar: 'Acabar' means 'to finish / end'. Acabar de + infinitive = to have just done something: Acabei de chegar = I've just arrived.
poder: 'Poder' = can / may (ability or permission): Posso entrar? Você pode me ajudar? For 'know how to', use 'saber': Eu sei nadar.
saber: 'Saber' = to know a fact or how to do something (Sei o endereço; Sei nadar). 'Conhecer' = to know / be familiar with a person, place or thing (Conheço a Ana; Conheço o Rio).
conhecer: 'Conhecer' = to know / be acquainted with a person, place or thing, or to meet for the first time (Conheci a Ana ontem). For facts and skills, use 'saber'.
querer: 'Querer' = to want (Quero um café). Polite requests often use 'queria' (imperfect) or 'gostaria' (conditional): Queria um café, por favor.
mesmo: 'Mesmo' = same (o mesmo livro), -self for emphasis (eu mesmo = I myself), and 'really / even' as an adverb (Sério mesmo? = really?; mesmo assim = even so).
então: 'Então' = so / then. Very common to connect ideas or start a sentence: Então, o que vamos fazer?
não: 'Não' = no / not; it goes before the verb (Eu não sei). Brazilians often double it for emphasis: Não sei, não. Before a noun it can mean 'non-': não fumante.
por favor: 'Por favor' = please. Softer requests use 'Você pode…?' or the imperfect 'queria'. Thank-yous: obrigado (said by men), obrigada (said by women), valeu (informal).
